item.title: Formalisation as a concrete manifestation of mathematical understanding
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: By formalising mathematics, not only we understand it better but we produce scientific output whose content is precisely this understanding. I will organise this argument by relating what brought me to formalising mathematics six years ago, and why I think that this beautiful human endeavour has very much to do with understanding mathematics, and very little with AI.
item.content:encoded:
Filippo A. E. Nuccio, Associate Professor at Université Saint-Étienne

AI use: none. See the full disclosure (“AI disclosure and licensing”) at the end of this post.

Disclaimer I am a maintainer of Mathlib, the main mathematical library of formalised mathematics in Lean, but all ideas expressed below are my own only; in no way are they supposed to represent an official view of the Mathlib community, nor of its governance.

Introduction

As the mathematical community is swamped by large amounts of results found by different LLMs, we’re reading more and more messages around three main pivots, often intertwined: that “mathematics is truly about understanding”; that those who are the most affected by this revolution are PhD students, or young colleagues in general; and that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are behaving badly, in one way or another. Somewhat unrelated to the above criticisms, we witness an increasing appearance of the words “formalisation” and, often, “Lean”. I believe that the four strands are related, perhaps in an unexpected way.

The overarching theme around which I’m going to develop my text is that understanding mathematics is a beautiful concept, but very hard to define. At which point can we say that we’ve understood it, and what does it really mean? Can we communicate understanding to colleagues or, even better, to students in a structured way? Can we produce a certificate that some understanding happened? Is there a reproducible outcome of this understanding? To what extent is mathematical understanding a scientific production rather than a method? Is this understanding subject to usual scientific scrutiny? Can we verify it?

I am going to argue that the bare-hand formalisation of mathematics is one answer to the above questions. By formalising mathematics, not only we understand it better but we produce scientific output whose content is precisely this understanding. I will organise this argument by relating what brought me to formalising mathematics six years ago, and why I think that this beautiful human endeavour has very much to do with understanding mathematics, and very little with AI.

A small digression: reasons to worry

Let’s pause for a moment, and look back at the first three points I mentioned above, namely: that mathematics is truly about understanding, that we care about the young generation, that these tech companies’ behaviour is bad and purely driven by economic targets. They remind me of another controversy.

I’ve long been an Open Access advocate, and I’m engaged with some organisations actively promoting it, from MathOA to the French Committee for Open Science. In this role, I’ve often argued that simply accusing the “usual three” Elsevier, Springer, Wiley of being the main obstacle to a full development of open access (in mathematics, or in any other science for that matter) is a red herring: it is our community, so the mathematicians, who put so much emphasis on publications lists and journal rankings. We are those who provide tenure, who promote young colleagues, who refer and distribute grants; and we’re the ones who decide to do so according to the list of shining publications in top (privately owned, often) journals: this approach values understanding very little, rather forcing our young, or less young, colleagues to publish as many papers and as quickly as possible in the top journals in order to obtain full recognition of their hard work. Unfortunately, spending PhD or Postdoc time trying to understand is something that our community has for too long valued way less than publishing in good Elsevier, or Springer, or Wiley journals. We took the easier path of declaring that mathematics was about publishing new results, that the problems came from three bad publishers whom we treated as the beasts, and we’ve refused to change our internal functioning model; yet, it was entirely within our hands.

I’ve heard time and again that we should do something to improve both the “publish or perish” stress imposed on ourselves (and, mostly, over our students’ shoulders), and to take back the power that big publishers can exercise upon our community: nonetheless, little has changed in the last fifteen years. I fear that the same might happen when I read about so many calls to “rethink our profession” in the aftermath of each large release of theorems proved by AIs. But unlike the publishing dead-end where we seem irremediably trapped, we’ve got here a practical action that can be taken: embrace formalisation as a full-fledged mathematical discipline tasked with organising what it means to understand an argument.

Understanding mathematics through its formalisation

To describe how this organisation could develop, let me start by spelling out another point leaving me sceptical at the idea that “mathematics is about understanding”, beyond its vagueness: mathematics cannot be about one thing, simply because it has been studied for more than 2.500 years, by hundreds of thousands of people, and a recent text by Gowers explain this perfectly. In the same vein, I will not dare stating what the true, intrinsic value of formalising mathematics is; but I will try to tell why I consider it a beautiful angle from which to regard mathematics, focusing more on understanding rather than on proving new theorems.

I will not provide any detail about it: I will content myself in saying that formalising mathematics in a proof assistant like Lean, Rocq, Isabelle, HOL-Light, Agda, etc., consists in writing definitions and statements in one of those languages, and then providing the code representing the proofs of the statements. Most of the time, neither of the two can be performed simply by following the informal exposition to be found in articles or monographs. Hence, I should rather say that formalising mathematics consists first in reflecting upon how to write definitions, statements and proofs; and, secondly in writing them down. More often than not, this reflection focuses on mathematical objects that have already been defined somewhere, in some form, and on proofs that already exist; but whose form is unsuited for the formalisation. This unsuitability might amount to inappropriate generality, to verbose computations hiding the core of the idea, to repeated argument hindering the identification of a common pattern. Since the production of new mathematical results is not its substance, the discipline has long faced the question of whether it really was part of mathematics.

When we co-founded, together with my friend and colleague Rob Lewis, the Annals of Formalized Mathematics, we wanted to draft the journal’s Aims and Scope and, helped by the two boards, we wrote, among our criteria, “The act of formalizing mathematics is not mechanical: it involves substantial mathematical insight in its own right, and it constitutes the essence of formalized mathematics”; and “Proof auditing, the act of checking that formal statements correspond correctly to their informal counterparts, is a difficult and inherently human part of reviewing formalized mathematics”. For me, these describe well what constitutes the scientific kernel of the formalisation of mathematics: and explains why it provides an excellent vehicle to communicate and to reason about mathematical understanding. By producing bare-hand formalised artefacts and by writing papers describing what we learn and discover through this activity we are turning understanding into something tangible.

Our formalisation activity typically focuses on looking at an established theorem, or a whole theory, and on trying to distil its understanding to the point where we can sanctify this distillation into a file, or within a whole library. This process I find incredibly pleasant and rewarding, especially because very often this distillation is a community effort: the Mathlib library currently (October 2026) contains two and a half millions of lines of code, written by hundreds of contributors, and it is only as valuable as the existence of the whole Mathlib community around it. We craft, in this manner, a concrete, structured, substantial witness of the community understanding of a topic. It goes without saying that almost every mathematical activity is deeply rooted in understanding, and this is by far not a unique feature of formalisation, nor its defining quality; my point is that the scientific outputs of this activity primarily solidify this understanding, instead of conveying it.

The discovery of this formalisation activity brought me tremendous joy: spending time reading beautiful (even if sometimes horribly written) papers and trying to produce new scientific outputs through their understanding was again my main activity, not an ancillary one that I could try to squeeze in between two attempts at proving my small new theorem. With this perspective, I believe that the production of humanly formalised mathematics in a proof assistant is an excellent way to sail some of the stormy waters we’re encountering: it will assist us in understanding the overabundance of results proven by AI and in creating a transmissible, teachable version of this understanding. As a by-product, it will ensure us that the reasoning beneath those mathematical arguments is sound.

Some thoughts on autoformalisation

I just wrote that getting assurance of the soundness of an argument is a by-product of formalisation. Yet, the pattern we’re observing is rather the following: one or several LLMs are prompted to attack a problem, they do so by producing an argument in the form of a written text and, alongside the text, these agents provide lengthy (Lean, say) code certifying the correctness of their argument. This formalisation performed by an LLM to certify that some argument is correct we call “autoformalisation”. Many colleagues or AI-companies consider this verification the main goal, rather than a by-product, of formalising mathematics in a proof assistant and I respect this position.

But, to my eyes, a huge collection of autoformalised mathematics stands in front of a smaller humanly formalised library like Mathlib as the invention of bookbinding compares to the invention of the press. Bound volumes are the way we experience the usefulness of the press, and they carry its impact in the form of printed pages organised handily and, often, harmonically. Nevertheless, most likely, the refined art of bookbinding would not exist hadn’t Gutenberg’s revolution seen the light of the day. Likewise, when a huge proof—perhaps produced by an LLM, or not—is autoformalised, its correctness is guaranteed (I am aware of technical issues about this guarantee, but let me gloss over them) and this we hold dear. But I look at this autoformalisation as one way of experiencing the usefulness and long-lasting pervasiveness of bare-hand formalisation, carrying its impact to the everyday life of (post?)-modern mathematics. The observation that almost all autoformalisation projects, so far, have been spelling out explicitly that they “rely on Mathlib” is perhaps a sign of such pervasiveness.

Conclusion

I wish more and more colleagues will join our formalisation community, enjoying the beauty of understanding mathematics—whomever or whatever shall it come from—through the painstaking and ever-rewarding activity of formalising it by hand, and discussing their formalisation efforts with even more colleagues and students. The outcomes will take the form of scientific productions contributing to frame the meaning that the broader mathematical community imparts to the idea of understanding, and I hope this might heal our terror that there’s no mathematics ahead of us.

AI disclosure and licensing

No form of AI has been used while producing this text. This text is licensed under a CC-BY 4.0 licence.

item.title: Sisyphus and the Sorcerer: An Existential Meditation at the Chalkboard
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: What becomes of a mathematical life arranged around proof when the stone rises without human hands? A meditation on Camus, Hilbert's paradise, and the unsettling shift from Sisyphean labour to superfluity—asking whether mathematical discovery can survive the loss of being humanly needed.
item.content:encoded:
Sajad Ahmad Sheikh, Assistant Professor of Mathematics at South Campus, University of Kashmir

In my twenties, I turned to mathematics partly because I could not bear the questions I was asking outside it. I had read enough existential philosophy to become suspicious of the purposes by which people arranged their lives, and enough literature to find that suspicion everywhere. Mathematics gave me something definite to do. A lemma could resist me for a week, but I knew what it would mean to make progress.

There was mercy in this. Whatever else remained uncertain, an argument had to hold. A contradiction could be located. An apparent impossibility might yield if I found the right way to approach it. I could spend an evening failing, go home with chalk on my cuffs, and still feel that the evening had possessed a shape.

Gradually, the refuge became a vocation. Mathematics acquired the intimacy that music or poetry has for those who live through it. A proof could remain with me long after I had put the book away. An unexpected connection could alter the mood of a day. There were pleasures here that I could scarcely explain to anyone outside the subject, and I came to depend on them more than I understood.

Now I find myself wondering what will become of those pleasures. The uncertainty from which mathematics once sheltered me has found its way to the chalkboard.

Camus held that there is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that it is suicide. At the chalkboard, an adaptation of his question suggests itself, the kind a mathematician makes only in jest, and only half in jest: Should I prove this theorem, or should I kill myself? It is a bad joke, and I know what it borrows. Camus meant the question of existence. Mine is smaller and more embarrassing: whether the life I arranged around proof is still worth arranging. A mathematician who compares his career to the problem of existence has probably spent too long indoors. I notice, all the same, how much the second question has begun to feel like the first.

* * *

In the myth, Sisyphus pushes his stone towards a summit it can never permanently occupy. He returns to his labour knowing what awaits him. Our mathematical version was more hospitable, and the difference is easy to miss: our stone did not roll back. What was proved stayed proved. There were many Sisyphuses on our mountain, and we had built a village around it.

Each of us carried what we could. Some moved small stones onto modest ledges. Others opened paths through difficult ground. A few brought enormous boulders to heights that had seemed inaccessible. Their names remained attached to the achievement, but the paths belonged to everyone. A result established by one generation became a foothold for the next. When Hilbert defended Cantor’s new infinities against their critics, he declared that no one should be able to drive us from the paradise Cantor had created. We took the sentence as a description of where we lived.

Most of us knew we would never reach the highest summits. That knowledge did remarkably little to spoil the undertaking. There was dignity in a small contribution, pleasure in understanding a difficult ascent, companionship in talking over a route that had defeated us. Even our failures took place within a common endeavour. Somewhere, someone was making progress, and the possibility remained that we might help.

The village had known alarms before. Russell found a crack in the foundations, and Gödel showed that the foundations could not vouch for themselves; Weyl is said to have remarked that God exists because mathematics is consistent, and the devil exists because we cannot prove it. In 1976 the four-colour theorem was settled with the help of more than a thousand hours of machine time, and people asked whether this was mathematics or merely its result. The classification of the finite simple groups lies scattered across hundreds of papers, and no single mind holds all of it. We absorbed these shocks and learned to call them history. In each case, the machine, or the sheer scale, stood at the edge of the work. Understanding still lived in the village.

* * *

Then a sorcerer appeared at the foot of the mountain.

He watched the villagers labour. Presently, he spoke a few words, and a stone rose from the ground.

At first, it was easy to remain unimpressed. The stone was small. The ascent had been made before. The sorcerer sometimes lost his grip or announced that a boulder had reached the summit when it had scarcely left the earth. Those who understood the mountain could point out his mistakes, and pointing them out restored a measure of confidence.

Then he lifted a heavier stone.

The confidence has become harder to restore.

The sorcerer has not lifted every stone. He has lifted enough to make the village listen whenever he speaks.

There is an awkwardness in calling him an intruder. The old stories have a better word for him: something we made. The rabbis’ golem is shaped from clay and woken by a word; Goethe’s apprentice speaks a spell he only half understands and cannot unsay. Our sorcerer was shaped from generations of proofs, from the patient exposition of teachers, from arguments polished by people who could not have imagined this use of their work. Human ingenuity built the machinery. If it eventually makes much of our intellectual labour unnecessary, the achievement will belong to our civilization. That prospect does not tell an individual mathematician how to feel about it.

I can admire what we have made and still be frightened by what it may ask us to relinquish.

The obvious reply is that the pleasure of mathematics was never dependent on being first. I know this from experience. I have spent happy hours understanding proofs whose authors died centuries ago. The discovery was theirs; something happened in me nonetheless. A beautiful argument does not become ugly because a machine produces it. Nor does another intelligence’s speed prevent me from thinking slowly.

But the reply is incomplete, and Thurston explains why. Mathematics, he argued, is not the accumulation of certified truths but the advance of human understanding. By that standard the danger is subtler than being outpaced. The question is less whether the sorcerer can prove the theorem than whether anyone will be able to tell us why it is true.

Consider what happens when a proof finally closes. The pleasure is private, but it is not solitary. Somewhere in it is the colleague who will raise an eyebrow, the student who will one day be shown the argument, the long line of people who left us the tools. Mathematical life has drawn on all of these at once: the private pleasure of understanding, the hope of finding something new, the recognition of one’s peers, the responsibility of teaching, the feeling of belonging to an undertaking that will outlast us. We do not know how easily they can be separated. We may discover that some of the pleasures we considered entirely inward depended on a world of other people who needed what we could do.

A colleague more gifted than I am does not abolish that world. There remain questions for different abilities, tasks distributed across a community, years in which understanding must be patiently acquired and passed on. But the word computer once named a person, often a woman at a desk, who calculated. Her profession did not end on a dramatic day. It simply stopped being offered. A system capable of undertaking an expanding share of our work could change the terms of participation for the whole community, and the question would reach beyond who gets the credit for a theorem. It would enter classrooms, appointments, apprenticeships, and the advice we give a young person willing to devote ten years to learning how to think.

What would we tell that person? Picture a child arriving at the foot of the mountain, asking what to carry and whether there will be a place on the slope. Weber told his students that every scientific achievement asks to be surpassed, and took for granted that the ones who surpass us are our pupils, or their pupils, so that being surpassed is a way of being continued. What becomes of that consolation when the surpassing needs no apprenticeship? Which promises could we still make to the child in good faith?

Here the unease outgrows the profession. Across centuries, we have treated the cultivation of intelligence as one of the strongest answers to the brevity of a human life. We build schools, preserve books, and ask the young to endure difficulty because understanding is worth the time it takes. Mathematics gives this conviction an unusually pure expression. A person with paper, patience, and sufficient ability might contribute something that no one had known before.

We are beginning to confront a possibility for which that inheritance has offered little preparation: the growth of knowledge may become increasingly independent of the long human education through which we have learned to value it. The institutions could persist for a while, along with their ceremonies and vocabulary, even as the reasons for entering them changed. A civilization might celebrate an extraordinary increase in its powers while struggling to explain to its children what their own powers were for.

This is a possibility, not an accomplished fact. Its uncertainty is part of its force. We must continue choosing projects, teaching students, and making lives inside a transition whose extent we cannot see.

* * *

Around the mountain, reassurance is readily available. There will always be harder problems, we are told. Humans will choose the questions. We will supply judgment, taste, meaning. Freed from the labour of proof, we will rise to a more creative relation with mathematics. Keynes, in 1930, imagined the day when the economic problem would be solved and warned that mankind would then meet its real and permanent problem: how to use its freedom. Arendt, a generation later, feared a society of labourers liberated from labour that had no higher activity ready to receive it. Release from toil, both knew, is not the same as knowing what the release is for.

I want to believe some of this. But I cannot see what entitles us to assign the higher ground to ourselves in advance. Formulating a question is also intellectual work. So is recognizing a fruitful definition, noticing an analogy, or deciding that a result matters. If our confidence rests on the claim that these activities must remain beyond the sorcerer, it rests on a boundary we have yet to establish.

There may indeed be new mountains. The sorcerer may see them first.

What I do believe is that the answer will not be handed down by the sorcerer. How much of the village survives will depend on what we choose to teach, to honour, and to pay for, and we have not yet chosen.

Another reassurance is more intimate: we can continue for our own pleasure. Let the machines advance the subject; we shall do mathematics as people play the piano at home, badly and with love. Chess players, and then players of Go, have lived through a version of this. Lee Sedol, retiring in 2019, said that even if he became the best of all human players there would remain an entity that could not be defeated. People still play. But chess never claimed to be discovery. There is nothing contemptible about the amateur’s life, and for many it could be a happy one. Still, the invitation asks us to accept a profound alteration in a vocation. Someone who hoped to help discover the world is being asked whether the private experience of discovery will suffice.

For some it will. I cannot yet answer for myself.

Camus gives us a Sisyphus who can look directly at his condition. The struggle itself towards the heights, he wrote, is enough to fill a man’s heart; one must imagine Sisyphus happy. I have leaned on that sentence for years. It assumes, I notice now, that the struggle is ours. Camus’s Sisyphus suffers futility, and futility can be defied. Ours would suffer something Camus did not have to imagine: superfluity. The stone rises, and it is no one’s hands that lift it. I do not know what defiance looks like against being merely unneeded.

Our difficulty is also that the condition keeps changing. The stone is still there this morning. By evening, it may have been carried elsewhere. We are asked to discover a durable attitude towards a future whose terms are revised with each announcement.

* * *

So Sisyphus sits down.

I am reluctant, now, to call his stillness meditation. That would lend it a wisdom he may not possess. He is in Beckett’s predicament, unable to go on and unable to do otherwise than go on, except that today, for the first time, the second half of the sentence is in doubt. His hands retain the habit of pressure. He knows the slope, the places where his footing is uncertain, the small adjustments by which an impossible weight can sometimes be moved. None of this knowledge has vanished. He cannot determine what to do with it.

Another stone passes overhead, and he finds himself talking, as people do when there is no one left to interrupt.

Was it all for nothing? Not the stone, since the stone was only ever a stone. The years. The mornings declined, the invitations refused, the holidays spent with a notebook open on his knee. A decade spent learning a language so that a few dozen people might read what he wrote in it. Was I wasting my time? Did I call it toil, and a complicated toil, so that it would sound like a vocation?

He tries the kind answers. You never did it to be first. The pleasure was real, and no one can send it back. But the other voice, the one with a mathematician’s cruelty towards loose reasoning, points out that the pleasure was real for every man who ever believed himself needed, and that the belief does not follow from the pleasure. Perhaps what you took for a calling was a very elaborate way of keeping busy. The toil was difficult, certainly. That is not the same as its having been necessary.

He has no counterexample ready. But he knows what to do with a claim he cannot refute: he looks for the hypothesis it quietly assumes. This one assumes that a thing is worth doing only if someone else needs it done. It assumes that the worth of the years lies in what they produced, and not in what they made of him. He is not sure he believes either assumption. He is not sure he does not. Not proven, he says aloud, an old verdict and an unsatisfying one, though it is the first honest thing anyone has said on the mountain all week.

The stone above him is out of sight now. He does not look up.

It is possible that he will get up tomorrow and find the old pleasure waiting. A difficult step may absorb him so completely that, for an hour, he forgets the sorcerer. There may be forms of companionship with this new intelligence that enlarge mathematical life beyond anything we can presently imagine. I cannot exclude them. I cannot honestly inhabit them yet.

Nor can I dismiss the other possibility: that mathematics will flourish while the human life gathered around it becomes harder to sustain. There may be more theorems, deeper theories, extraordinary new connections, and fewer occasions on which a person feels that their years of preparation have brought them somewhere they are needed. Even wonder might change when we can no longer follow the route by which knowledge arrives.

Sisyphus sits at the foot of the mountain, his hands still curved to the shape of the stone. Around him, the village continues its work, though now each ascent is watched with a question that no one quite knows how to ask. Perhaps the sorcerer will open paths along which human curiosity can travel further than it ever could alone. Perhaps the paths will remain, beautiful and deserted, while discovery passes beyond the reach of those who once gave their lives to it. From where Sisyphus sits, these futures share the same horizon.

For so long, he knew what morning required of him. Even despair had a task to return to. Now the stone rises without his hands, and the hours ahead have become strangely difficult to imagine. He may stand, choose another stone, or walk away from the mountain towards something for which the village has no name.

The sorcerer continues his work. Sisyphus has yet to move.

Received 9 October 2026.

item.title: On Expositions, and the Navier–Stokes Generation of PhD Students
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: As part of the “Navier–Stokes generation” of PhD students, I feel lots of uncertainty, excitement, and anxiety, perhaps all at once. Reading Littlewood’s Miscellany, however, reminded me that maths is full of little gems, that are perhaps a bit overlooked amongst the AI hype.
item.content:encoded:
Yifu Zhang, first-year maths PhD at Imperial College London

AI is used only for spelling/grammar checks, and for compiling and plotting the data in the chart.

When I applied for my PhD last year, I certainly didn’t expect that just before I started it, there had been a millennium problem drama. Amongst my friends, I’m now part of the “Navier–Stokes generation” of PhD students. There are a lot of uncertainties: What will we do as PhDs if an AI can do frontier-level mathematics? Will the journal system remain intact? Will there be a position for me when I graduate?

I’m a numerical analyst-in-training, and some of the problems I work on seem less tangible and less well-defined than those on the pure side. Nevertheless, we felt the shockwaves from the proof of the Crouzeix conjecture and, more recently, the new upper bound on the complexity of matrix multiplication.

There are numerous blogs and essays that have sprouted this year, and many in the community have turned to the thoughts of great mathematicians, notably Thurston’s in On Proof and Progress in Mathematics, which has been widely discussed, for example by Grant Sanderson. Another well-known (more controversial) piece is Hardy’s A Mathematician’s Apology, as referenced (though by no means concurred with) by Kevin Buzzard.

Speaking of Hardy, allow me a small digression. According to “an excellent colleague” of Harald Bohr, “Nowadays, there are only three really great English mathematicians”. The first of them is naturally Hardy, but I personally find Littlewood, the second of them, more agreeable1.

A Mathematician’s Miscellany was written by Littlewood and later edited by Béla Bollobás. I want to share here a few more short quotes from this genius book:

“It is very hard to make a random selection of stars. If, for example, you see a star (with the naked eye) it is probably bright.”

“J. J. Sylvester sent a paper to the London Mathematical Society. His covering letter explained, as usual, that this was the most important result in the subject for 20 years. The Secretary replied that he agreed entirely with Sylvester’s opinion of the paper; but Sylvester had actually published the result in the L.M.S. five years before.”

“When Trinity once had some wine at a lowish price, but not satisfactory and also not selling, they doubled the price, whereupon the idle rich bought it all up.”

The Miscellany has no direct bearing on the current situation, but to me it brings more clarity than some of the serious, timely statements: it keeps me grounded and curbs my tendency to think about AI all the time.

Many in the community have rightly argued for the necessity of the explanatory side of mathematics. However, from the chart, we are seeing only an increase in the AI discussions2. With the current discussion about human understanding of maths, shouldn’t there be a flood of new mathematical expositions as well? The Miscellany, to me, represents the best of them: quirky stories about mathematicians and their lives; small, delicious mathematical nuggets that piqued Littlewood’s interest; or just arbitrary, casual thoughts during research.

There are many important initiatives about the role of AI in maths, and statements are put out every day to respond to the new reality. They are certainly vital voices that need to be heard, but I argue that the less flashy, more casual expositions should also be promoted. They:

  1. make difficult mathematics digestible for others, particularly for new PhD students and researchers from other areas who may find more specialised material difficult. An example I personally benefited from even as an undergrad is this.
  2. they (typically) acknowledge their sources well, linking to other useful, digestible materials. This is not only proper practice for academia, but also serve as excellent pointers for their readers. It works both ways: papers/essays that are frequently referenced are probably good explainers themselves.
  3. encourage public outreach efforts, demonstrating the community’s commitment to public understanding and putting the explanatory side of mathematics into practice.
  4. give the public and early career researchers (e.g. the N–S generation) more confidence that the community is not single-mindedly focused on AI and that the field is still alive with mathematical activity. This helps balance out the anxiety, which, though justified, affect how we navigate the new landscape.

Back to being the “Navier–Stokes generation”. As junior mathematicians, we face many uncertainties but also many opportunities, so it is natural to think a lot about AI. Reading the Miscellany, however, reminded me of what inspired me to study mathematics. This may seem idealistic and naïve to many, but there are interesting people, good stories, and fun maths in our field, and they are worth recording.

  1. The final one is, of course, Hardy–Littlewood. ︎
  2. The stats here are very limited by the tools available to me; they only include the partial data that Claude could find, and the format is limited to blogs. This leaves out many other forms of exposition, such as the brilliant videos from SoME. Nevertheless, I hope the point still stands. ︎

Received 16 October 2026, revised 25 October 2026.

item.title: What Mathematicians Want?
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: What do you want from AI as a mathematician? If we could plan it all from scratch, would you like to see it back as a spellchecker and nothing more, or do you want it to do research at the highest level? As a computer scientist, I would like to understand the positions and feelings around the desired form the community wants it to have.
item.content:encoded:
Reuven Peleg, M.Sc student for Computer Science at Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel

AI Disclosure: This post was written entirely by me, AI was used to proofread the final draft.

The current big wave of AI for Math discourse was forced upon the Mathematical community. The big labs got more and more advanced results on conjecture proving, triggering all kinds of reactions, feelings and backfire reactions. The main focus of discussion was how to react to events: Should the community cooperate with AI labs, or scrutinize them? How should journals and conferences treat AI-generated papers?

I would like to ask a different question: What do you want from AI as a mathematician? I find it intellectually interesting, but also practical for me, as I don’t want to conduct research that steps on someone’s toe instead of helping. As a Master’s student interested deeply in AI For Math and planning out his future career, I want to politely ask the professionals in it what their needs or expectations are.

One answer I got is “leave us alone”. Some professionals say they want to use AI for literature review, spellcheck, maybe some assistance in coding if necessary, and that’s it. Just like an artist who wants the robots to put down the brushes, they want the human-centric experience of creation and exploration.

On the other side of the spectrum, there seems to be a camp of pro-AI mathematicians that are generally happy about machine-discovered math, with some specific concern: About reliability of the claims, copyright, attribution and norms, ownership, responsibility for papers, et cetera. Once it’s settled, they want to have the most powerful, fast, cheap and reliable Math AI that can be built.

I don’t have a clear understanding on how big each camp is, what are the positions in between, or what aspect I miss in the needs of the community. I also hope there is a way for AI to fit in Math research, maybe in a way I can’t envision as an outsider. So I am asking: If you could steer the AI research and have your dream outcome for the field, what would it be?

Received 9 October 2026.

item.title: Nothing More than Tools?
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: My psychological defenses kept retreating as frontier LLMs entered mathematical research. Are these models really nothing more than tools? I must rethink what gives meaning to my mathematical life. The core is what I would call toolization—keeping humans at the crucial nodes of the intellectual activity while outsourcing parts of the reasoning.
item.content:encoded:
Chenmin Sun, CNRS junior researcher at UPEC

I have subscribed to a commercial LLM for more than three years, at $20 per month. As a Chinese native living abroad, I used it to polish my language, to seek advice on daily life concerns, and to chat about almost anything. It was a toy, sometimes a friend who could patiently listen to me, and most of the time a shortcut tool. It entered my mathematical life at the beginning of 2025, when I could play with it in the context of university-level problem-solving, interactively learning papers from other domains in which I had little expertise. The model, accessible to me through that cheap subscription, evolved at almost a constant pace. It became my custom-made super search engine, calculator, verifier and reliable Wikipedia.

As a PDE researcher dealing with many estimates, I had always expected a real-time research assistant embedded in my workflow while editing a long paper in LaTeX. It would perfectly understand the logic flow I was working on, helping me to deal with tedious case checks and basic estimates where the guiding principle is clear. At that time (even at the beginning of 2026), LLM agents were not that popular in my community, and it was difficult—at least for me—to implement the above workflow. AI for mathematics remained distant from my research. It was not yet the assistant I had hoped for.

The situation changed dramatically over the past few months. While news about AI-solved Erdős problems kept coming, the storm was getting closer to all of us. The first wave of preprints emerged on arXiv, with many AI-solved (or heavily-assisted) mid-to-high-profile problems in every domain of mathematics. It was the time of GPT-5.5, and since then we have seen GPT-5.6, Fable 5, Astra… People devised a dazzling array of ways to play with these models: first, all kinds of prompting tricks that seemed to lack intellectual depth; then workflow construction and the distillation of various skills. In early 2026, building agent tools still posed a certain barrier to entry for non-programmers. But once Codex and ChatGPT were deeply integrated, an amateur who knew nothing about mathematics or programming could, with nothing more than naive prompts, keep a model working until an oracle-like proof was spat out by the computer. So, are these agents built on frontier LLMs really nothing more than tools?

By common sense, a tool is characterized by a specific range of uses and a determinate capability—or at least by a capability that improves steadily within a predictable range. Motivated by a desire to understand the performance of a frontier commercial model, I tried one a couple of months ago. My psychological defenses kept retreating: An early version (GPT-5.5) could not solve any of the problems in a small set from my personal collection. The situation changed when GPT-5.6 arrived. To understand which “hard problems” were worth working on, I started testing several open problems in my field—fortunately without success. Later in the summer, I heard about a fancy way of working—so-called “drawing cards” for major open problems. People around me were drawing cards, and succeeding. From my perspective, this way of working is hallucinogenic. We immerse ourselves in a virtual world as commanders of a massive army, commanding well-equipped soldiers (agents) to attack day after day until they exhaust their ammunition (tokens), with only very high-level intervention. Even pure curiosity—the will to know the truth—chases us, and hallucination emerges in our minds: we must know; we will know. An invisible force catches us: well-organized prompts must be sent before leaving home, during dinner with family, and before sleep. Does any tool make us addicted like that?

The ethical consequences are even more serious. If a result is obtained through long but almost context-free prompts, whose name should appear on the paper? Opinions differ. From my perspective, authorship of a research article—as distinct from an expository article—should be reserved for those who contribute creative intellectual input. And in the case of automatic problem-solving, where the model works essentially on its own to close the loop of theorem-proving and verification, why should it be credited only as a tool?

This is no longer hypothetical. On October 6, 2026, before the community could adapt to the new paradigm at a reasonable pace, OpenAI released mathematical manuscripts grouped into 372 result families, including candidate solutions to high-profile problems across all areas of mathematics. The news came like a cluster of nuclear bombs, destroying the old landscape of mathematics, yet few survivors could foresee the new horizon.

This is the landmark event that forces me to confront an existential crisis. There is no more room for psychological retreat. I must rethink what gives meaning to my mathematical life.

Without getting involved in the controversial commentary on similar events, or in how we should act collectively, I would rather share my individual thoughts on how I want to adapt to the advance of AI in my career. Since nobody can predict the future, I should state that what I am going to discuss should not be taken as a standard or judgement I am imposing on others, and these views will steadily evolve over time.

The core is what I would call toolization. More specifically, the model is assigned a bounded range of local tasks, while humans pilot the direction at crucial nodes of the search tree. However, the definition of local tasks and the direction of the search vary from person to person, and will also evolve over time. A tricky integral at the undergraduate level is a local task for an experienced researcher who understands the mechanism behind it, but it remains a good training exercise in a master’s internship project. We can take it for granted that we may outsource labor within our ability. For instance, suppose there are two scale-invariant estimates for a given integral, A and B. We applied A, while the model applied B to get a better bound. It does a nice job as a co-pilot, and we advance more quickly. In current PDE research, what is essential is the architecture and the mechanism of how things work. For example, one must conjecture a blow-up profile, construct an ansatz to close the bootstrap, design fine norms to encode linear/multilinear effects, and guess Lyapunov functionals. We pilot these directions, and suitable AI tools (not just prompting LLMs) would allow us to quickly test ideas and counterexamples, to code for numerical experiments, to use knowledge from other domains, and to carry out the dirty work.

Mathematical development is based on the compression of concepts. Just as nowadays researchers directly use theorems of Banach spaces or classical analysis without opening the black box of the proof, AI tools allow us to work on modules, compressing not only a specific theorem in the literature, but also low-to-middle levels of reasoning. Yet, unlike traditional compression, which rests on clear definitions, the compression of AI reasoning requires novel conceptualization, so that similar mechanisms can be generalized and reused. As part or even all of the reasoning is outsourced, conceptualization becomes a new kind of cognitive work for human mathematicians, increasingly decoupled from the problem-solving process.

In another direction with the same principle, an LLM is a mobile library and a custom-made teacher. Learning ideas and techniques from other fields (even outside mathematics) in which we have no expertise, digesting new results (human or AI-produced), and coding become more convenient. This way, again, it is our consciousness that decides what to understand, and how deeply to understand it.

I acknowledge that it is always difficult to get toolization right, given the continuously increasing mathematical capabilities of LLMs. In the research process, a more delicate situation arises when an LLM contributes a key idea. It leads us towards a new direction—one that turns out to be successful—that we had not previously considered. If that happens, I consider the LLM a collaborator who deserves credit. This would make me excited, because I could reach further horizons that would otherwise be difficult to find on my own, while also making me feel a sense of loss. After all, making creative contributions to the process of discovery is a principal motivation for why I do mathematics.

As a double-edged sword, long interaction with an LLM might cause reliance on it that deskills us, eroding our abilities and intuition. But I think this effect can only be evaluated a posteriori, over time. I could periodically ask myself a set of questions: Do I gain a better understanding of my subject? Am I still able to do AI-free mathematics when I am on the plane? What cognitive tasks can I safely outsource to a model? Ideally, these questions would help me maintain both intellectual growth and independence. The critical dose of AI usage depends on the person. As we now have models with a wide range of capabilities, choice and discipline become a new personal challenge.

Today, it is becoming clearer that the industrialization of mathematics is coming; nobody is sure whether it will be a golden age of discovery or a regression of civilization. It depends on the collective narrative and on individual practice. We need time to adapt to the new paradigm, to reach a certain consensus within our community, and to rebuild our confidence. The destructive impact is real, but one thing is certain: mathematics is not a closed system, and human curiosity about the universe is unbounded.

Received 10 October 2026.

item.title: Postdoc Hiring in the Age of AI: What Still Matters (and a Call for More Advice from Those Doing the Hiring)
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Alessio Figalli and Sobhan Seyfaddini, drawing on their experience hiring postdocs, explain how they will evaluate candidates this year in light of recent AI advances. They will privilege substance over publication counts and expect an in-depth mathematical conversation at interview. More advice from those doing the hiring will be added here.
item.content:encoded:
SERIES · Part of our application-season series for people considering a PhD, doing a PhD or looking for a postdoc. We expect a few more contributions like this one from people involved in hiring this year, and welcome others (send us yours); they will be added to this post as they arrive. Applicants can ask questions in the comments below. Each contribution reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

Alessio Figalli and Sobhan Seyfaddini, Professors at ETH Zurich

Drawing on our experience as past and current members of postdoctoral hiring committees, we would like to share our perspective on how to evaluate postdoctoral candidates in the age of AI.

AI does not change what we ultimately want to assess in a candidate: the depth of their mathematical understanding, the substance of their own contributions, and their potential to develop new ideas.

At the initial shortlisting stage, we expect recommendation letters and CVs to play an important role, but we do not regard publication counts alone as a reliable guide to a candidate’s potential. We are more interested in the substance of the work and in what the application reveals about the candidate’s own contributions, ideas, and development as a mathematician. Where possible, we may also examine selected papers more closely to gain a better understanding of the mathematical ideas involved and how they are presented.

For shortlisted candidates, the interview will be crucial for assessing their mathematical understanding and judgment more directly.
Can they explain the ideas behind their results, why the arguments work, and where the difficulties lie?
Can they discuss what they tried, what failed, and which questions remain open?
We would also like to understand how they see their work in a broader mathematical context, why they consider it significant, and what they regard as their own main contributions. We expect that a talk followed by an in-depth discussion will give us a good sense of each candidate’s mathematical understanding, maturity, and approach to research.

Our advice to applicants is therefore to make their own contributions clear in their applications and to be prepared to discuss their work in depth, since a thoughtful and honest mathematical conversation can reveal far more than a publication count. While the ways in which we assess candidates may evolve as the tools available to mathematicians change, our emphasis will remain on mathematical understanding, originality, and research potential.

Received 5 November 2026.

item.title: It’s a great time to be an amateur mathematician
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “In early August, I was at TIFR Mumbai for an ‘AI for Math’ conference. This is one of many such events happening in mathematics departments all over the world in recent times. Among the speakers was Dinesh Thakur. In his talk, he described how he had received an email from an auto mechanic in France about a conjecture attributed to him. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Nihar Gargava, Postdoctoral researcher at Université Paris-Saclay

PS: I used AI for speech-to-text, proofreading, and locating references. I thank Dinesh Thakur for comments on an earlier draft.

In early August, I was at TIFR Mumbai for an “AI for Math” conference1. This is one of many such events happening in mathematics departments all over the world in recent times. Among the speakers was Dinesh Thakur. In his talk, he described how he had received an email from an auto mechanic in France about a conjecture attributed to him2. The email came with a disproof of this conjecture about primes over function fields that he had written about in 2015. What was surreal about this incident was that the person sending this counterexample did not even know what finite fields are! He had just asked Claude (Opus 4.8) to find a “precisely stated conjecture about polynomials with some examples worked out and something that can be checked by computations”, quoting Dinesh. Dinesh told us that eventually the author did learn more about the problem via more prompting. The preprint is currently on arXiv3.

The reaction from the audience was quite dramatic. There was laughter in the room, but also shock and disbelief. Two reactions that I recall were “what does it mean to have any expertise anymore?” and “it’s a great time to be an amateur mathematician”. By mid-October, these stories are becoming more common, and I expect that trend to continue. I would like to present my thoughts about this.

Mathematics is full of delightful stories of outsiders making an impact. The most famous is that of Ramanujan, whose letters to Hardy still bring pleasure to the mathematics community even after repeated readings. It seems to me that every professional mathematician at one point in their career must have gotten an email from a Ramanujan-wannabe. Most of these are bogus emails and we don’t bother replying to them. But now these emails are getting smarter and more intricate because of AI. Firstly, a crackpot with a crazy claim can now instead run his ideas through a language model and spare a mathematician a few bytes of mailbox space. Secondly, a mathematician can receive an interesting piece of mathematics tailor-made to appeal to their taste.

I recently had my Ramanujan-Hardy moment myself when Michael Simkin, who lives in Georgia (the country), sent me a new lower bound on sphere packings in high dimensions. The model’s write-up was an astonishing mess that would be difficult to read for any poor soul having to go through it, perhaps more so for Michael, who is mostly an outsider to research mathematics. He asked AI to recommend a mathematician who could verify the result, and it gave him my name.

When Michael reached out to me, I did get interested. At first, I thought he was Michael Simkin, the lecturer at MIT. But after a few emails I realized this was someone else. The output from the model had nice tricks to make progress on some of the ideas that I had long abandoned. So I asked Michael if he would like to coauthor this with me. I also (with his permission) added a PhD student to this project—Matthias Gröbner (because who owns AI-generated results?). The preprint is now out on arXiv4.

I wanted to understand what had drawn Michael to this problem, so we talked about it. Michael told me that he had been interested in mathematics since high school. He grew up in Tel Aviv and had even won an IMO bronze medal in his teenage years5. Mathematics has kept him going in life, even though his parents could not afford university education for him. Michael is now known for interesting life form constructions in Conway’s Game of Life6. For the past few years, he had been living as a digital nomad all over the world, finally settling in Georgia. These days he works part-time for a brain imaging center. He is proud of his AI-prompting skills and wants to keep helping mathematicians.

I asked Michael what he thought about expertise in mathematics and whether he felt that he could replace mathematicians with his AI chats. He had an answer that I found pretty nice. Coming from a software engineering background, he knows the feeling of AI being able to do the job better than humans. But he adds “as a programmer, I still have skills that are important but I cannot pinpoint what they are”. I guess this is quite close to what mathematicians feel.

The post-AI age could be a good time for mathematicians to reach out to people like Michael. It could be of mutual benefit. Not only do people outside want to understand what the mathematics produced by the models is saying, but we might also need them to understand how the public sees and interacts with mathematics. Human mathematicians should exist to talk about mathematics to humans, and the humans are finally reaching out in our mailboxes. They are finally speaking our language and learning about our work at their own pace. I think we should engage with at least some of them as a kind of individual outreach. AI might be taking away some of the fun parts of our jobs, but there might be new opportunities in our mailboxes.

The following are my thoughts as of now, and I expect to keep updating them as interactions between professional and hobbyist mathematicians become more common in the AI era.

Advice to hobbyist mathematicians

It might look as though mathematicians spend most of their time going through the gory details of individual lemmas and propositions in papers. In practice, however, mathematicians often focus on the few parts of a paper that are genuinely novel or interesting, without checking every detail once they are convinced that the result should be true. Much of the communication of mathematical ideas also happens through conversations between mathematicians, who have developed a shared language for talking about what matters in a proof. My advice to hobbyist mathematicians is to be patient with and respectful of this process. Try to understand how mathematicians communicate with each other, and learn to talk about your own ideas in that language. Being imperfect is okay, but trying will earn you a lot of respect.

Advice to professional mathematicians

The goals of hobbyist mathematicians might sometimes seem outrageous or too far removed from those of a professional researcher. They might be especially keen to be the first to prove a theorem, improve a bound, or put a result into the world just to have their name on it. But these could be respectable ambitions and, pre-AI, were (often tacitly) shared by many professional mathematicians. Even when we do not share precisely the post-AI goals of human understanding, there is still an opportunity for collaboration between hobbyists and professionals. Professional mathematicians should be mindful of their own priorities while respecting hobbyists’ expectations.

Addendum: Michael’s new homepage is 7

  1. Tata Institute of Fundamental Research. AI for Math workshop programme. (2026). ︎
  2. D. S. Thakur. Fermat-Wilson supercongruences, arithmetic derivatives and strange factorizations. arXiv:2211.01076 (2022). ︎
  3. D. Niedbala Giraudin. A counterexample to a conjecture of Thakur on Carlitz-Wieferich primes. arXiv:2607.15305 (2026). ︎
  4. N. Gargava, M. Gröbner, & M. Simkin. A cyclotomic gluing construction for lattice sphere packings. arXiv:2610.12619 (2026). ︎
  5. International Mathematical Olympiad. Individual results – Israel. ︎
  6. LifeWiki contributors. Michael Simkin. ︎
  7. M. Simkin. Personal homepage. ︎

item.title: I’m Not Done Doing Math! Don’t Ignore Me!
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “But I am still interested in doing math. I still think my research direction has genuine merit, and I still feel like I have more mathematics to give to the world. Thanks to AI, it is now feasible for someone like me to keep going.” […]
item.content:encoded:
Anonymous, Math PhD student

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

I am about to graduate with a math PhD, with zero published papers, and a subpar thesis that’s just barely enough for me to graduate.

I have no illusions that I am on the same intellectual tier as the tenured professors, postdocs, and PhD students much more successful than me writing on this blog. I am no Yitang Zhang. I readily admit that I am a low-level mathematician compared to even the peers in my department. And much of this is my own fault. Significant stretches of my time in the program were spent procrastinating and being distracted, not to mention just plain being stuck on a project because I wasn’t good enough.

Realistically, I will not, and should not, be getting a research postdoc. I will end up in an overloaded teaching position or working a regular 9-to-5 job. And I do not have contempt for this future. I am sure I will manage to find a job that is fulfilling for me.

Under the old rules of academia, my life in mathematical research was over. I was supposed to quietly pack up my stuff, and leave research mathematics to the REAL mathematicians.

But I am still interested in doing math. I still think my research direction has genuine merit, and I still feel like I have more mathematics to give to the world. Thanks to AI, it is now feasible for someone like me to keep going. With language models accelerating the time-consuming parts of research, it is realistic for someone carrying a heavy teaching load or working a day job to produce novel, interesting mathematics in the little free time they have.

That is what I am going to try to do. And what is wrong with that?

I wanted to write this down because when I read essays here, whether pro-AI or anti-AI, people like me aren’t considered a part of the conversation.

We have an opportunity right now to ‘catch’ the people who have fallen by the wayside. People who just barely survived their PhD program and still have good ideas. Or people with just a Master’s or a Bachelor’s in mathematics who didn’t want to go through the grueling 5+ years of low pay for a PhD. Or those that went through years of postdoc positions and failed to secure a tenure-track job. We, the people outside of research academia that still wish to continue with mathematical research, exist!

But almost every conversation among established researchers seems to forget that. This is understandable because, before AI, many of us could not feasibly do serious research mathematics outside of a research position. Research math is incredibly time-consuming. Even if someone had a novel mathematical insight, keeping up with the latest literature, checking citations, and writing things up in an understandable, presentable way was a time-consuming process. It was not feasible to do without a lengthy dedicated research time in their schedule, afforded by a research position. We were not considered “real mathematicians” for a good, understandable reason. (There are exceptions, of course. Those outside of research jobs have produced a great deal of amazing research before AI. But we must admit that it is now MUCH EASIER to do research math outside of an academic position.)

Now, with the advent of AI, it IS realistic for us to continue participating in mathematical research.

So could we be brought back into the conversation?

Because right now, when I read through the posts on this blog, people like us are completely ignored:

  • I see reports from elite gatherings like the Harvard CMSA summit on Math and AI, or calls for societies to set norms. Will those boards and summits ever include people like me? Will they care about the opinions of an overloaded teaching faculty member just wanting to continue exploring the direction of their thesis? Or the person doing math research in their free time after their 9-to-5? I am afraid that these organizations will just be another society of already successful mathematicians writing rules for themselves.
  • There is some panic that AI will create a torrent of papers and there simply won’t be enough qualified people to peer-review them. Really? There aren’t enough people to review them? Thousands of math PhDs graduate every year without continuing a research career. Is there really a shortage of capable people, or is our definition of “capable” severely restricted? With AI, it is now much easier for those without research positions to keep up with the latest developments in their fields. Would that not drastically INCREASE the number of qualified peer reviewers?
  • Several pro-AI posts suggest that because AI makes writing papers too easy, we should stop writing papers or devalue them in favor of live seminar talks and in-person workshops. Do people realize how exclusionary this is? It is a luxury that can only be afforded by those with grants and dedicated time off for travel.
  • I see professors warning that because of AI, we might “lose an entire generation of mathematicians”, while others decry that AI will reduce math from a profession to a mere “hobby” done in people’s spare time. Where was this panic when the academic job market was throwing away the vast majority of every graduating PhD class for decades? And why is doing math in your spare time, for zero money and zero career credit, treated with such contempt?

I have lost the game of academic research careers, and I have made peace with that fact. What frustrates me is that the mathematical research establishment pretend I don’t exist. When a tool finally comes along that lets me keep doing the thing I love, making small but real contributions to my field from outside of a research position, I continue to be ignored. Instead, one side is telling me that my work doesn’t count for using AI, while the other side talks only about how it can be directed to better serve and preserve the scant few dedicated research positions.

It is telling that even in a fictional utopian vision of mathematics in 2038, set in a literal post-scarcity world, one can only imagine the mathematical community through the eyes of... an ETH Zurich professor and a postdoc heading to a three-month retreat in Princeton. Wow. Just wow. Even in the wildest, most utopian fantasies of the future, people like me don’t exist.

Received 1 November 2026.

item.title: Futures of Maths Launch
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Today we launch Futures of Maths, a new, living platform that asks the mathematics community about the most pressing questions around maths and AI.
item.content:encoded:
Francesco Fournier-Facio, Assistant Professor at Heriot-Watt University; Yara Kyrychenko, Research Fellow at University of Cambridge (St John’s College); Jon Roozenbeek, Associate Professor at University of Cambridge and VU Amsterdam; Julian Wykowski, Postdoctoral Researcher at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology

Today we launch Futures of Maths, a new, living platform that asks active research mathematicians about the most pressing questions around maths and AI. A string of solutions to famous maths problems, found with the help of AI, has provoked a great deal of discussion among research mathematicians. We built Futures of Maths to understand how mathematicians are dealing with this change in their research and teaching, and where they see the field heading.

How it works. The platform shows you short statements about maths and AI. You rate each one from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”, or skip it, and you can mark the ones you find exceptionally important. Once you have answered, you see how everyone has rated the statement so far. You don’t have to finish in one go: you can leave and come back at any time. Most importantly, you can post your own statements. A moderator checks each one, and then everyone else can rate it, so the set of statements keeps evolving with the community’s input.

Results. Once we have collected enough responses, we will publish the results and make them available to the community. We will post again on Proofs and Prompts when this happens.

Who can participate. You can take part if you are 18 or older and have at least one article published in the last 5 years in a mathematics journal, meaning one indexed by zbMATH Open (recently accepted articles also count). The quickest way in is to sign in with ORCID. The article must be on your public ORCID record, added by Crossref. Articles you enter yourself don’t count. If it isn’t there, accept Crossref’s permission request in your ORCID inbox and make the work public. If that doesn’t work, for example because your article is accepted but not yet published, you can request a manual review from your institutional email address. We review these case by case.
We appreciate that this is only an approximation of what an active research mathematician is, but we chose it for its simplicity, objectivity and efficient verifiability. We welcome proposals of alternative criteria that cover a more representative sample, and have these same three qualities, they could be implemented in future iterations.

Privacy. The survey is anonymous. Verification happens on a separate website, and the survey itself never learns your name, email address or ORCID iD. When you first register, you receive a personal link that lets you return as often as you like as the consultation evolves. Please save this link. We can’t look it up or resend it, because that is what keeps you anonymous. Questions about yourself are optional, under “My session”, and you can withdraw your answers at any time.

Inviting wide participation. The results will only be meaningful if a large and diverse group of people takes part, both proposing statements and rating them. Please share this widely, and especially with people whose point of view you feel is underrepresented in the discussion on maths and AI.

If you have any suggestions or feature requests, please leave them in the comments!

Received 5 November 2026.

item.title: Reject the Neurosis, and Terrible Messaging, of our Loudest Voices — The Case for (Ir)rational Optimism
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “If you look up AI and math on any news site, you will read statements including ‘AI is destroying careers’ or ‘AI is nuking entire areas of math’ or even a prominent Field’s medalist saying ‘I cried so hard due to AI in math that I woke up my daughter’. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Anonymous, Postdoc

If you look up AI and math on any news site, you will read statements including “AI is destroying careers” or “AI is nuking entire areas of math” or even a prominent Field’s medalist saying “I cried so hard due to AI in math that I woke up my daughter”. The news loves a good headline, and these extreme statements make for good headlines. Underneath these articles is the comment section, with many comments hostile to mathematicians. One comment read “Imagine being a seven year old and your father waking you up to cry that other people did math problems.” This comment, hostile to mathematics (and arguably bad faith), I think sums up a very common reaction of non-mathematicians to some of these articles. I wanted to argue with this commenter, but I realized that this reaction was, on some level, perfectly reasonable if you just read the article and were not a mathematician.

It is no secret that graduate students can be stressed out and neurotic. I have been talking to younger mathematicians, and some are taking the rhetoric of senior mathematicians very seriously. I feel badly for them — some are incredibly depressed. I’m not going to tell people how to feel, because this is pointless. However, I do try to be more balanced than senior mathematicians have been — both because I think it is correct, but also because I have been disgusted by poor leadership.

The purpose of this essay is to implore senior mathematicians to tone down the extreme rhetoric, especially when communicating with the media and with junior mathematicians. I am encouraging this both because I believe these extremes aren’t true, but more importantly because it is bad leadership. It is like going into battle, even if you’re all going to die, your captain shouldn’t cry to you about it.

One major effect AI will have is forcing us to move on from well-trodden ground. The Riemann hypothesis has been around since…well…Riemann. The Navier-Stokes equations were introduced in the early to mid 1800s. Since then, these problems have accumulated an immense amount of prestige. Maybe it is time to move on? There are new questions to ask, there are new theories to develop, and new math to do. It seems like a lot of the neurosis comes from senior mathematicians who have attached an inordinate amount of self-worth to solving specific, well-formulated, and difficult conjectures. This is just one style of math, and it should not be seen as the entirety of math. AI will force a shift away from this style, which will ultimately lower the prestige attached to certain areas. However, in my personal opinion, this is a very good thing. I welcome this shift.

A second major effect AI will have is an increase in the number of papers, particularly incremental or “slop” papers. This is unequivocally bad. This may have a silver lining though — hopefully paper counts will be devalued, and paper quality will be valued more. This is a good thing.

A third major shift, related to the second, is that we can no longer trust someone’s papers to accurately represent their understanding or ability. This, again, is bad. However, similarly, I hope that this makes other things emphasized more in assessment — chalk talks, qualifying exams and coursework in grad school, informal conversations, and so on. The grad school standard of publication being the most important has, in my opinion, gotten a bit out of control. One thing a PhD should qualify you to do, is to teach mathematics. At the bare minimum, a person with a PhD in mathematics should be able to teach any undergraduate mathematics class or core graduate mathematics class (analysis, algebra, and geometry) with little difficulty. In reality, I don’t know how common this is. I hope AI devalues “novel contribution” and increases the value on having a solid foundation of core areas of mathematics.

Beyond any of these specifics, I have a very strong prior in the belief “nothing ever happens”. Mathematics has been around for thousands of years; it has undergone many changes. This will be yet another change, and mathematics will come out the other side alive.

If you still aren’t convinced, then could you at least tone it down a touch when talking to the media and younger mathematicians? If we really are marching towards the mathematical equivalent of nuclear armageddon, it is the responsibility of senior mathematicians to maintain some level of calm.
